title: How is StringBuffer thread-safe?
shortTitle: How is StringBuffer thread-safe compared to String and StringBuilder?
keyPoints: StringBuffer methods (append, insert, delete) are synchronized – only one thread at a time
StringBuilder has the same API but NO synchronization – faster for single-threaded use
String is thread-safe by being immutable – no shared mutable state
In modern Java, StringBuilder + proper design (thread-local building) is preferred over StringBuffer
Understanding this concept is essential for Java interviews at senior level

s1_definition.oneliner: StringBuffer's methods are synchronized. Only one thread can modify it at a time. StringBuilder is identical but unsynchronized and faster. Use StringBuilder by default.
s1_definition.profdef:
Thread safety comparison:

- **String:** Thread-safe by immutability (no state changes).
- **StringBuffer:** Thread-safe by synchronization (every method is synchronized).
- **StringBuilder:** NOT thread-safe. Fastest for single-threaded code.
s1_definition.analogy: String is a printed receipt (read-only, any number of people can read it). StringBuffer is a shared whiteboard with a lock (one person writes at a time). StringBuilder is a personal whiteboard (fast, no locking, one person only).

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  String:        immutable → thread-safe (no changes possible)
  StringBuffer:  synchronized methods → thread-safe (one writer at a time)
  StringBuilder: no synchronization → NOT thread-safe (fastest)

  Modern: each thread gets its own StringBuilder → no sharing → no need for StringBuffer
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
StringBuffer is thread-safe because its methods are synchronized. Only one thread can modify it at a time. StringBuilder has the same API but no synchronization, making it faster. In modern Java, use StringBuilder by default and avoid sharing it across threads.

One sentence to remember: StringBuffer is synchronized (thread-safe), StringBuilder is not (faster) – use StringBuilder and avoid sharing.
